We benchmark ACK-gated censored passive feedback against active proofs in 750 IEEE 802.15.4 runs on 30 new fixtures, with naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery increases from 71.28% to 75.94%, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls while total modeled radio energy rises slightly. The controls do not establish a unique censoring or attention advantage. A separate 180-run experiment tests frozen policies over authenticated messages and node-local records. Attention delivers 81.61% in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping, without an established advantage over greedy or multilayer-perceptron routing. Serial-interface testing identifies and corrects a receive-time freshness error. Earlier UART-to-radio firmware runs on four emulated Cortex-M3 boards; neural inference and cryptography execute on the host PC. Each host-policy control delivers ten of ten packets. A further 240-run factorial study separates proof traffic from evidence handling; adding proofs reduces delivery by 6.11 percentage points with always-on listening. A fixed-point MCU actor reduces signed-receipt deadline misses; a separate source-authenticated receipt profile meets its tested deadlines while retaining deferred public signatures. An exploratory 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing service debt. The contribution is a traceable comparison of feedback mechanisms and transport boundaries; the evidence does not establish sustained operation, physical-board performance, measured energy consumption or absolute deadline compliance.

before: ACK-gated censored passive feedback passed the prespecified replacement test on 30 new fixtures, improving blackhole delivery over active proofs by 4.67 percentage points. The matched controls establish neither a unique censoring effect nor an attention advantage. In the separate 180-run authenticated transport study, frozen policies operate on received wire state and local service records without an established attention benefit. Serial-interface testing corrected a receive-time error, and four emulated Cortex-M3 boards execute the compiled UART-to-radio bridge while inference and cryptography run on the host in that earlier fixture. The 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing source debt. Together, these results define the benchmark’s supported feedback comparison and deployment boundary: absolute service compliance, physical-board operation, physical on-board policy/crypto execution and measured energy remain unvalidated. The 240-run factorial extension identifies a proof-traffic delivery penalty with always-on listening, while severe loss under periodic sleeping limits transfer of that finding. Isolated Cortex-M3 execution verifies actor outputs and cryptographic primitives, not a complete embedded radio system. A four-node emulated live-path pilot now performs routing and authentication inside the MCU, including longer private-key runs. Fixed-point inference improves emulated latency, but signed receipts still miss the 90 ms target. A separate source-only MAC receipt meets the tested source deadlines while retaining deferred public proofs; the two endpoints provide different verification properties.
after:
ACK-gated censored passive feedback improves blackhole delivery over active proofs by 4.67 percentage points in the prespecified thirty-fixture benchmark. Matched controls establish neither a unique censoring effect nor neural-policy superiority. The separate 180-run authenticated transfer study likewise shows no established attention advantage, while the 240-run factorial extension identifies a proof-traffic penalty under always-on listening. These findings apply to the declared feedback, traffic and radio models.
Behavior change exposes a different boundary. In the 600-run Cooja delayed condition, active proofs deliver 79.11%, censored feedback 32.94% and naive feedback 54.89%; censored feedback with proof generation enabled delivers 32.83%. Censoring alone cannot reduce earlier positive trust when later observations disappear. Fixed-point MCU execution and fast private receipts improve narrower execution paths, but the original 90 ms signed-receipt target remains unmet. Physical RF, measured energy, production key storage and deployment performance remain unvalidated.

before: Earlier architecture comparisons found no joint advantage over a multilayer perceptron of similar capacity. A subsequent 600-run telemetry study likewise found no advantage after correction for multiple testing and exposed the traffic cost of active proofs. Both stages and their raw outputs are retained. They motivated the present comparison of receipt-assisted passive feedback with active proofs, subject to prespecified margins against a frozen-prior control on new fixtures.

before: The benchmark supports replacing the tested active-proof mechanism within its prespecified margins. Because eligibility and expiry rules change together with control traffic, the observed difference cannot be assigned to proof airtime alone. Comparisons with naive passive and frozen prior do not establish a unique censoring effect after correction. Retaining the earlier unsuccessful architecture comparisons prevents the feedback result from being recast as evidence for neural-policy superiority.
